\chapter{-ista --- Jobs You Can Already Read}
\label{ch:ista}
\hlchaptermodality{53}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can read an -ista word as English -ist without being taught it.}

I can read an -ista word as English -ist without being taught it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[-ista]{-ista}

\label{lesson:ES-C09-ista}



\begin{quote}
What does \emph{-ante} make? (\textbf{The one doing it}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I am a student.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Soy estudiante}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a job you can already read}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Spanish \emph{-ista} is English \emph{-ist}.}
\end{quote}

Greek \emph{\textbf{-istēs}} named the doer of an action. Latin borrowed it, and Spanish and English both still use it — so this ending needs almost no learning.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\emph{artista} & \textbf{artist} \\
\emph{dentista} & \textbf{dentist} \\
\emph{turista} & \textbf{tourist} \\
\emph{periodista} & \textbf{journalist} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three of those four you could read before this chapter opened. That is the point: \textbf{the ending is doing the work, not your memory.}

The fourth is the interesting one. \emph{Periodista} is not \emph{periodist} — it is built on \emph{periódico}, a \textbf{newspaper}, which is a \textbf{periodical}, something that comes round at a \emph{period}. The ending is regular; the root is the surprise.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: -ista never changes}]
Like \emph{-ante}, an \emph{-ista} word is the same for a man or a woman — and it keeps its \emph{-a} either way:

\begin{quote}
\emph{Él es artista.}  ·  \emph{Ella es artista.}
\end{quote}

The \emph{-a} is not feminine here. It is just how the word ends. Only the article moves: \emph{el artista}, \emph{la artista}.

And still no \emph{un}: \emph{Soy artista}, not \emph{Soy un artista}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{artista, dentista, turista}
  \item \emph{Soy} — and one of them
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{-ista} in English? (\emph{\textbf{-ist}}.)

Does it change for a woman? (\textbf{No.})
\end{tcolorbox}
